The weaknesses are typical of a category piece, not an amateur one. The monochrome electric-blue 'tech liquid' look is very familiar. The type is a plain wordmark plus a widely tracked 'EVOLUTION' that sits on the image rather than working with it.
gaps: Give the type a role. 'EVOLUTION' as letterspaced caps floating in the centre is the most generic move in the piece. It should come out of the fluid or be shaped by it.
Break the all-blue palette with at least one second temperature or an accent. As it stands, it sits alongside a hundred other 'liquid tech' launch films.
Make the concept specific to AR glasses. Water-as-evolution could sell any device. B owns its world, a fully ASCII universe, in a way this does not.

tells: A complete, committed system: every image is built from ASCII and code glyphs ($, <, #, 0/1, Bitcoin marks). The typography is the illustration, which is an idea only a piece about digital money could own.
Deliberate, unusual palette: saturated International-Klein-like blue with white type only. It is brave and recognisable at once.

The density and variety of the frames point to procedural tooling built for the job. There is a walking figure, a coin streaking through glyph flow, an orbiting glyph planet, padlocks beside scrolling source code, and a grid of coins turning in differing states.
The labels ('<<Crypto is...', 'Faster') are white-box UI tags that work as captions inside the system, and the code snippets mention the client's engine. This is designed copy, not slide text.
gaps: The figure and padlock silhouettes in frames 1 and 4 are the least crafted elements, close to stock icons rendered in ASCII. Give them custom drawing.
Add more depth or lighting variation inside the ASCII field so a few frames stop reading as flat screen-filled patterns.
Give the end card or the lock-up a stronger typographic climax. The fragments sampled here never land on one hero typographic poster.

tells: Strong, motivated light: hard raking window shadows, warm bounce, believable gold and glass refraction, and paper or plaster grain on the ground. These are look-dev decisions, not defaults.
A consistent material language (glass plus brushed gold) carried through the coin, the phone, the tiled floor, the tablet and the stacked coins. Each frame works as a still.
The client typography (J.P.Morgan wordmark, serif balance '$2.45M') sits inside the UI on the device. It is restrained and on-brand, but it has no expressive role.

Risks of the corporate-fintech template show: glyph-in-a-glowing-disc icons (padlock, cart, circle), the same lone hero object on a beige surface in most frames, and motion implied mostly as echo trails.
gaps: The idea stops at 'premium glass and gold fintech icons'. It needs a concept specific to the bank's payments story, not generic padlock and cart pictograms.
Vary the staging. Four of five frames are a single object on the same beige plane under the same window light, so the choreography reads as a series of stills.
Give typography a real part in the film beyond UI dressing, through scale, kinetic type or type-as-material in glass and gold.

tells: Heavy simulation work: fluid, refraction, caustics and particles all behave plausibly across frames, which is costly hand-built CG rather than a template
The product dissolves into liquid and comes back, so there is a transformation arc across the frames instead of one repeated layout
Close-up macro frames (the gel-like temple arm, the cell-like bubble field) vary the scale and keep it from being a turntable
Weakness: the electric-blue liquid tech-launch look is a familiar genre, and the type is plain (bold grotesk wordmark, widely tracked thin 'EVOLUTION' centred over the busy image)
gaps: The look is a stock 'liquid blue product launch' that could sell any device. Tie the liquid metaphor to something specific to AR glasses, such as light, vision or overlaying worlds
The type is an afterthought. 'EVOLUTION' in wide-tracked thin caps on top of busy texture is a cliché. Give the titles a system that sits inside the material, like refracted or embedded in the liquid
The palette is one blue throughout. Add a counter-colour or a shift in value so the frames have a progression and a climax

tells: The whole film is built from ASCII and monospace glyphs, so type and image are the same material. That is a committed system with a point of view
A saturated International-Klein-style blue with white glyphs is a deliberate, ownable palette, not a default dark theme

The frames vary a lot: a walking figure, a coin with flow fields, a glyph planet with orbit rings, padlocks beside scrolling code, and a grid of spinning coins. That shows choreography and pacing, not one layout repeated
Small details reward a pause: inverted-label callouts ('<<Crypto is...', 'Faster'), pseudo-code that reads as copy, and glyph density used to model 3D form
Weakness: the crypto iconography (₿, $, padlocks) is literal, and the ASCII aesthetic is something of a current trend
gaps: The subject icons are on-the-nose (coins, padlocks, dollar signs). Push one frame to an image that only this system could make, rather than a crypto symbol drawn in ASCII
Depth is mostly simulated through density. A layer of real light, glow or bloom on the glyphs would give it the material richness that C has
The coin-grid finale is the weakest frame and reads as a contact sheet. Build to a single composed end frame

defects: The lever-frame shot is a glossy 3D render with saturated red, blue and white handles. It breaks the flat signal-diagram language used in every other shot.
Frame 2 catches the headline 'One API call.' mid-wipe as illegible fragments. The headline arrives after the lever action, so the reveal order is muddled.
The 'webhook at every signal' beat holds nearly still across the 1/6 s pair. Only the train nudges, so it reads as dead air on a 3.8 s shot.
The 'Instant settlement' title is a static boxed card over moving tracks. It covers the busiest action and is the kind of lower-third a template would use.
Several type systems compete: a geometric sans headline, tiny mono webhook labels, wide-tracked caps and a mono typewriter. The webhook labels are close to unreadable at delivery size.
The surfaces are flat vector at 100%: amber glow halos but no grain, light falloff or texture. The dark green background is close to banding.
In the settlement shot the trains slide at constant velocity with no easing or spacing variation. It reads as a loop, not a burst.
gaps: Motion: the train metaphor never gets weight. Trains need to accelerate off the signal, overshoot and settle at Bank B, and the switch points need mechanical snap. The webhook nodes should fire one after another as the train passes, building to a real peak, but they currently pop on as a static diagram. Shots are long (median 2.8 s) with holds that don't earn their time.

Visual system: the 3D lever shot and the boxed text card break the invariant. A top studio would keep one material, the lit schematic railway, across every shot. The lever frame would be built as signal-box diagram art, and the type would sit on the track rather than in a card.

Sound and finish: the bed is busy, with dense clicks and repeated filtered whoosh sweeps, but it is undifferentiated. There are few dynamic drops before the hits, and the sweeps repeat the same gesture. The final bell resolve is nice but synthetic-sounding. The picture needs grain, light falloff on the glows and a richer tonal range to match the sound's ambition.
